article.title: New Deal Majority
article.author: John Peeler
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Since the Civil War, scholars have found a persistent pattern in party competition in this country. One party tends to win the majority of votes nationally for several consecutive elections. Then some critical event such as a depression leads a critical mass of voters to switch loyalties. The former minority party becomes the normal majority. After the Civil War, the Republicans were the normal majority, narrowly until 1896, then overwhelmingly until the Great Depression. The shock of the Depression and the vigor of the New Deal response then established the Democrats as the normal majority until the late 1960s. The Civil Rights movement, the unpopular Vietnam War, and widespread protests eroded the Democratic hegemony, allowing the narrow election of Richard Nixon in 1968. The 1970s were a transitional period marked by the Watergate scandal and the resignation of President Nixon. An era of Republican dominance emerged with Ronald Reagan’s election in 1980, but lasted only until George H.W. Bush’s defeat by Bill Clinton in 1992. Related: When Democracy Strikes Back: Trump, Orbán, and Pinochet Since 1992, there has been no nationally dominant party. Clinton lost his congressional majority in 1994, but was easily reelected in 1996. In 2000, voters were almost evenly divided in an election decided by the Supreme Court in Bush v. Gore . Bush and Obama were each reelected, but then saw their opposition capture the presidency. Trump and Biden were each denied reelection, and probably the Republican successor to Trump will lose to the Democrat in 2028. A key feature of the earlier periods of party hegemony was that most voters identified with either the Republicans or the Democrats. Independent voters were relatively few. Now, however, in this era of no party hegemony, the weight of independents has increased. By definition, independents are not attached to either party (though many may lean toward one or the other). In this year’s election, independents determined outcomes in contest after contest. The Democrats could not have achieved their strong majorities without independent voters. The Democrats now have a strategic choice. They can accept the logic of the current no-hegemony era, and just play for the victory in 2028. That would entail highlighting the misdeeds and unpopularity of Trump and his party, and pursuing policies to undo the many evils that Trump has perpetrated. That’s the line of least resistance. But that’s a virtual guarantee that the Democratic president elected in 2028 will be defeated in 2032. And most likely, s/he will lose the congressional majorities in the midterms of 2030. The reason lies in a fundamental reality of American life over the last fifty years. Our society has grown steadily more economically unequal. Today average people can barely make ends meet with two full-time workers. People are more and more indebted. They are less likely to afford to buy a home. As successive elected governments in this century have failed to address this economic reality, they have been turned out of office: Bush II, Obama, Trump I, Biden, and (probably) Trump II’s successor. Related: Trump's Political Collapse Was Entirely His Own Making The second choice the Democrats have is to undertake to rectify this half-century injustice, to take concrete steps rapidly improving the well-being and security of most people. That will include reversing the tax cuts for the wealthy that Republicans since Reagan have enacted. Medicare for All would be a key accomplishment, but minimally, Obamacare and Medicaid should have the Trump cuts reversed. Social Security should be put on a stable basis. These are just some of the major reforms that should be undertaken to make life better for most people. If the Democrats pursue this second course, they will have the chance to establish a new period of Democratic hegemony like that which started with the New Deal. The Republicans, meanwhile, must choose between being a right-wing MAGA minority party, and, on the other hand, contesting the independents they lost in this year’s election. If they choose the latter, that would be good for our democracy: for democracy to work in the long term, it needs at least two parties competing, both committed to democracy. Now, sadly, only one party is committed to democracy.
